revision.body:
Where can a probability sit?

A probability measures how likely one named event is. A value of 0 means impossible, \(\frac{1}{2}\) means an even chance, and 1 means certain.

Check the outcome described before judging its chance. The same probability can be written in different ways, such as \(\frac{1}{4}=0.25=25\%\).

What goes in the denominator?

When the individual outcomes are equally likely, use \(\frac{\text{number of favourable outcomes}}{\text{number of all possible outcomes}}\).

Count everything that might be chosen. Then count the items that match the event. Read each relevant row of a frequency table.

How can I find the chance of the opposite?

An event and its complement cover every outcome. Their probabilities add to 1.

Find the chance of the easier event, then subtract it from 1 where the question asks for its complement. If a table of distinct outcomes has one missing probability, subtract all the given probabilities from 1.

Quick worked example

A machine assigns integers from 1 to 6, each equally likely. Consider the event that the selected number is at most 6. Which description matches the event?

  1. Certain
  2. Impossible
  3. Unlikely, but possible
  4. Equally likely to happen or not happen

Every possible outcome meets the event.

Its position on the scale is \(1\). This means certain.

sections.title: How do the results estimate probability?
sections.label: Observations

blocks.html: Relative frequency is the proportion of actual trials in which an event occurred. It estimates the chance under similar conditions.

figure.caption: The total includes outcomes that did and did not meet the event.

blocks.title: Practise the method
blocks.html: Divide the observed success count by the number of trials. To pool comparable results, add the successes and add the trial totals before dividing.

blocks.title: Estimate probability from repeated observations
blocks.prompt: A paper propeller lands upright in 22 of 88 trials. Use relative frequency to estimate the probability of an upright landing. Give an exact fraction or decimal.
blocks.hint: Relative frequency means the fraction of trials that actually met the event.
blocks.solution:
Use the observed results. Divide upright landings by the total number of trials, including unsuccessful landings.

This estimates the chance in similar trials. Repeating the experiment may give a different observed relative frequency.

The answer is \(\frac{1}{4}\).

retry.feedback: This is the fraction of landings that were not upright.

blocks.html: Unequal groups should not automatically get the same weight. Count every trial once.

blocks.hint: The runs have different trial counts, so pool the trials to give each trial equal weight.

retry.feedback: A simple average gives the two runs equal weight. Here the individual trials should have equal weight.

sections.title: How do I turn a chance into an expected count?
sections.label: Prediction

blocks.html: The expected frequency is \(\text{number of trials}\times\text{probability per trial}\).

blocks.title: Practise the method
blocks.html: Identify the event, check which trials are being predicted, then multiply the future trial count by the chance per trial.

blocks.title: Predict an expected number of outcomes
blocks.prompt: A calibration test fails with probability \(\frac{2}{5}\) on each trial. For 80 similar trials, find the expected number of failures.
blocks.hint: Multiply, because you want the chance applied across the whole group of trials.
blocks.solution:
Multiply the number of future trials by the probability on one trial. Use \(80\times \frac{2}{5}\).

This is an expected count, rather than a guarantee of how many failures will occur.

The answer is \(32\).

retry.feedback: This is the probability of one failure rather than the expected number of failures.
That is the expected number that pass. Count failures.

sections.title: Do unequal counts prove a process is biased?
sections.label: Fair experiments

blocks.html: A fair two-outcome model gives the two named outcomes equal chances. Random outcomes can still produce different observed counts.

blocks.title: Practise the method
blocks.html: Use randomly chosen trials under consistent conditions. Collect comparable evidence before concluding that one outcome is favoured.

blocks.title: Distinguish random variation from evidence of bias
blocks.prompt: A counter-making test has two possible results. The supplier claims the results are equally likely. In one run there are 48 red results and 58 black results. Which conclusion is justified from this single run?

options.A: Different observed counts can occur even when the two chances are equal.
options.B: The different counts prove the supplier is wrong.
options.C: The red result has no chance of occurring again.
options.D: Each future run must have the same counts as this one.

blocks.hint: A random result can vary even when the rules and chances do not change.
blocks.solution:
Fair means equal probabilities for the two outcomes, not fixed observed counts.

A single nonmatching count does not prove bias. More comparable trials can improve an estimate.

retry.feedback: A fair process does not make the observed results exactly equal each time.
A red result occurred, and both outcomes can still occur on the next trial.
Observed counts can vary between runs even when the chance stays fixed.

revision.body:
How do I make a sample-space grid?

Write first outcomes down the side and second outcomes across the top. Each cell represents one ordered pair.

Enter the sum or product in every cell if the question asks for one. When the pairs have equal chances, count matching cells and divide by all cells.

Which outcomes meet the wording?

‘Greater than’ leaves out equality. ‘At least’ includes equality.

Mark all satisfying cells before counting. Leave unmatched cells in the total number of outcomes.

Replacing the first item makes it available again for the second draw.

List the same choices for both draws. Include the diagonal of equal labels when suitable, then test the condition.

512131415
613141516

Exactly 3 ordered pairs give the required total. Count those cells in the grid.

blocks.title: Practise the method

blocks.title: Read the required regions of two overlapping sets
blocks.prompt: At a school, 25 students attend Art, 24 attend Coding and 8 attend both clubs. There are 50 students altogether. One is chosen at random. Find the probability that this student attends at least one of these clubs. Give an exact fraction or decimal.
blocks.hint: Separate the overlap, the two single-club regions and the outside region before counting.
blocks.solution:
Adding the two group totals counts the 8 students in both groups twice. Subtract their overlap once.

Use 41 students who attend at least one club out of 50.

The answer is \(\frac{41}{50}\).

retry.feedback: That is the overlap alone. Read the exact event in the question.
The overlap has been counted twice.

igcse-0580-prob-trees-with-replacement.description: Complete a tree for two draws with replacement and use multiplication and addition to combine complete outcomes.

sections.title: What changes when I put the first item back?
sections.label: Reset

blocks.html: With replacement, the first item is returned before the next selection. The second draw uses the original counts.

figure.alt: First stage, Blue: 12 out of 32, Amber: 20 out of 32. After Blue, Blue: 12 out of 32, Amber: 20 out of 32. After Amber, Blue: 12 out of 32, Amber: 20 out of 32.
figure.caption: Both second-stage splits repeat the original group counts.

blocks.title: Practise the method
blocks.html: Draw two first branches. From the end of each branch, draw the next possibilities. Each split shows chances out of the full count for that draw.

blocks.title: Follow and combine paths on a tree
blocks.prompt: A bag contains 13 blue discs and 4 amber discs. Two discs are drawn at random. The first is replaced before the second draw. Find the probability that both discs are blue. Give an exact fraction or decimal.
blocks.hint: List the complete first-and-second outcomes that meet the event. Use the correct branch counts for the second draw.
blocks.solution:
The first disc is put back. The branch counts stay the same.

The blue-then-blue path is \(\frac{13}{17}\) multiplied by \(\frac{13}{17}\).

The answer is \(\frac{169}{289}\).

retry.feedback: That is the chance for the first draw only. Follow both branches.

blocks.html: A second-draw probability belongs to a branch from its first result. Make both second splits.

blocks.title: Supply a missing branch probability
blocks.prompt: A jar contains 9 blue discs and 5 amber discs. Two discs are drawn at random. The first disc is put back. Find the missing probability of drawing an amber disc second, given that an amber disc was drawn first. Give an exact fraction or decimal.
blocks.hint: Keep the second split after the stated first colour. Find the new count for the requested colour.
blocks.solution:
On the chosen second split, there are 5 amber discs and 9 of the other colour.

The two outgoing probabilities add to 1. Subtract \(\frac{9}{14}\) from 1.

The answer is \(\frac{5}{14}\).

retry.feedback: That value is on the other branch. The two outgoing branch probabilities add to 1.

revision.body:
What if I already know the first branch?

When the first result is given, work from that node. The probabilities leaving it describe the possible next results.

Ignore the branch leading to the other node. Read the second-stage proportion from the given group.

How do I work backwards from the outcome?

If the final result is known, keep every complete path with that result. These paths can have different probabilities.

Multiply along the retained paths. Divide the relevant path probability by the sum of the retained path probabilities.

How do I tell a joint event from a condition?

A joint event names what must happen at both stages of the original trial. A condition limits what still counts as possible.

For a joint event use the full path's probability. If a final event is known, use its total probability as the new denominator.

Quick worked example

A selector chooses bag A with probability \(\frac{8}{17}\) and bag B otherwise. Bag A contains 7 copper tiles out of 11. Bag B contains 6 copper tiles out of 14. Once a bag is chosen, a tile is drawn at random from it. It is known that the tile is copper. Find the probability the selector chose bag A. Give an exact fraction or decimal.

The two ways to reach copper are bag A then copper and bag B then copper. Their probabilities are \(\frac{56}{187}\) and \(\frac{27}{119}\).

Only copper outcomes are still possible. The total weight of those two paths is \(\frac{689}{1309}\). Divide the bag A copper path's weight by that total.

The answer is \(\frac{392}{689}\).
